claim: The central complex of the insect midbrain is thought to coordinate insect guidance strategies.
source: The central complex of the insect midbrain is thought to coordinate insect guidance strategies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general proposition about the central complex's role.

claim: A previous model (Sun et al. 2020) of visual navigation can generalize to olfactory navigation and its coordination with other guidance in flies and ants.
source: Here, we assess the capacity of our previous model (Sun et al. 2020) of visual navigation to generalise to olfactory navigation and its coordination with other guidance in flies and ants.
evidence: The abstract states this as the main finding of the current study.

claim: A biologically plausible neural copy-and-shift mechanism ensures sensory information is presented in a format compatible with the insect steering circuit regardless of its source.
source: We show that fundamental to this capacity is the use of a biologically plausible neural copy-and-shift mechanism that ensures sensory information is presented in a format compatible with the insect steering circuit regardless of its source.
evidence: This is presented as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: The copy-and-shift mechanism allows the transfer of cues from unstable/egocentric to stable/geocentric frames of reference.
source: Moreover, the same mechanism is shown to allow the transfer cues from unstable/egocentric to stable/geocentric frames of reference, providing a first account of the mechanism by which foraging insects robustly recover from environmental disturbances.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: The copy-and-shift mechanism provides the first account of how foraging insects robustly recover from environmental disturbances.
source: Moreover, the same mechanism is shown to allow the transfer cues from unstable/egocentric to stable/geocentric frames of reference, providing a first account of the mechanism by which foraging insects robustly recover from environmental disturbances.
evidence: This is claimed as a novel contribution in the abstract.

claim: Central complex circuits can be flexibly repurposed by different insect navigators to address their unique ecological needs.
source: We propose that these circuits can be flexibly repurposed by different insect navigators to address their unique ecological needs.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal in the abstract.

claim: The insect head-direction system in the CX tracks the animal's current heading relative to external cues.
source: The evidence to support this hypothesis includes the discovery of the insect head-direction system in the CX that tracks the animal's current heading relative to external (Heinze, 2014; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Kim et al., 2019; Hardcastle et al., 2021) or self-motion (Green et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2017) cues
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The insect head-direction system in the CX tracks the animal's current heading relative to self-motion cues.
source: The evidence to support this hypothesis includes the discovery of the insect head-direction system in the CX that tracks the animal's current heading relative to external (Heinze, 2014; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Kim et al., 2019; Hardcastle et al., 2021) or self-motion (Green et al., 2017; Turner-Evans et al., 2017) cues
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The fan-shaped body (FB) region of the CX is innervated with sensory information relevant to different orientation strategies.
source: the innervation of the fan-shaped body (FB) region of the CX with sensory information relevant to different orientation strategies (Hu et al., 2018; Franconville et al., 2018; Hulse et al., 2021; Shiozaki et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The columnar structure of the CX is well suited to computing desired headings for vector navigation tasks.
source: the well-preserved columnar structure that is well suited to computing desired headings for vector navigation tasks (Stone et al., 2017; Honkanen et al., 2019; Le Moël et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A neural steering circuit in the FB is capable of computing motor commands that reduce the offset between the current heading and a desired heading.
source: and the identification of a neural steering circuit in the FB capable of computing motor commands that reduce the offset between the current heading and a desired heading (Stone et al., 2017; Honkanen et al., 2019; Rayshubskiy, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Computational models of CX architecture have produced realistic path integration (PI) behaviors.
source: Computational models of this architecture have produced realistic path integration (PI) (Stone et al., 2017; Gkanias et al., 2019) and trap-lining behaviours (Le Moël et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: Computational models of CX architecture have produced realistic trap-lining behaviors.
source: Computational models of this architecture have produced realistic path integration (PI) (Stone et al., 2017; Gkanias et al., 2019) and trap-lining behaviours (Le Moël et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Simple conceptual extensions of CX models could account for long-distance migratory behavior.
source: and simple conceptual extensions have been outlined that could account for long-distance migratory behaviour (Honkanen et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For the CX to be considered a general navigation centre, it must be capable of generating gradient ascent/descent behaviours that rely on spatially varying but rotationally invariant sensory cues.
source: Yet, for the CX to be considered a general navigation centre, it must additionally be capable of (i) generating gradient ascent/descent behaviours that rely on spatially varying but rotationally invariant sensory cues (e.g. odour gradients)
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for the CX to be a general navigation center.

claim: For the CX to be considered a general navigation centre, it must be capable of coordinating competing guidance systems into a single meaningful motor command.
source: Yet, for the CX to be considered a general navigation centre, it must additionally be capable of (i) generating gradient ascent/descent behaviours that rely on spatially varying but rotationally invariant sensory cues (e.g. odour gradients), (ii) coordinating competing guidance systems into a single meaningful motor command
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for the CX to be a general navigation center.

claim: For the CX to be considered a general navigation centre, it must be capable of generalizing across sensory modalities and task spaces.
source: Yet, for the CX to be considered a general navigation centre, it must additionally be capable of (i) generating gradient ascent/descent behaviours that rely on spatially varying but rotationally invariant sensory cues (e.g. odour gradients), (ii) coordinating competing guidance systems into a single meaningful motor command, and (iii) generalise across sensory modalities and task spaces.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for the CX to be a general navigation center.

claim: The steering circuit can be adapted to ascent gradients of visual familiarity when augmented by a neural 'copy-and-shift' mechanism.
source: We recently demonstrated how the steering circuit could be adapted to ascent gradients of visual familiarity when augmented by a neural 'copy-and-shift' mechanism that converts temporal changes in spatially sampled sensory information into an orientation signal (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: The copy-and-shift mechanism converts temporal changes in spatially sampled sensory information into an orientation signal.
source: We recently demonstrated how the steering circuit could be adapted to ascent gradients of visual familiarity when augmented by a neural 'copy-and-shift' mechanism that converts temporal changes in spatially sampled sensory information into an orientation signal (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a functional description of the mechanism.

claim: The copy-and-shift mechanism copies the animal's current heading from the head-direction cells in the protocerebral bridge (PB) to desired heading networks in the FB.
source: Specifically, the mechanism firstly copies the animal's current heading from the head-direction cells in the protocerebral bridge (PB) to desired heading networks in the FB.
evidence: This describes the 'copy' stage of the mechanism.

claim: The copy-and-shift mechanism shifts the signal in proportion to any undesired change in sensory valence as measured by the mushroom body (MB) output neurons.
source: At the same time, the signal undergoes a lateral shift in proportion to any undesired change in sensory valence as measured by the mushroom body (MB) output neurons (Aso et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the 'shift' stage of the mechanism with citations.

claim: The animal will continue on its current heading until an undesirable change in sensory valence is experienced.
source: Thus, the animal will continue on its current heading until an undesirable change in sensory valence is experienced at which point the shift mechanism will create an offset between the current and desired headings, causing the steering circuit to initiate a change of direction.
evidence: This describes the behavioral consequence of the mechanism.

claim: When an undesirable change in sensory valence is experienced, the shift mechanism creates an offset between the current and desired headings, causing the steering circuit to initiate a change of direction.
source: Thus, the animal will continue on its current heading until an undesirable change in sensory valence is experienced at which point the shift mechanism will create an offset between the current and desired headings, causing the steering circuit to initiate a change of direction.
evidence: This describes the behavioral consequence of the mechanism.

claim: Head-direction cells transmit their output into the ring structures of the central body.
source: head-direction cells are known to transmit their output into the ring structures of the central body (Stone et al., 2017; Honkanen et al., 2019) as needed for copy stage
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neural mechanisms that laterally shift the head-direction cells in response to sensory feedback are well established.
source: and neural mechanisms that laterally shift the head-direction cells in response to sensory feedback (e.g. the self-motion cues [Turner-Evans et al., 2017; Green et al., 2017], the visual cues [Kim et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2019]) are well established as required for the shift stage.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The complete 'copy-and-shift' mechanism explains how the CX steering circuit could exploit sensory gradients that provide no instantaneous orientation information for navigation.
source: Crucially, the complete 'copy-and-shift' mechanism explains how the CX steering circuit (see Figure 1) could exploit sensory gradients that provide no instantaneous orientation information for navigation.
evidence: This is stated as a key insight of the mechanism.

claim: The model includes a contextual-switching mechanism that triggers specific guidance strategies depending on the context.
source: We also demonstrated neural mechanisms that coordinate between different guidance strategies (Sun et al., 2020). Specifically we added a contextual-switching mechanism (see Figure 1) that triggers specific guidance strategies depending on the context, for example, switching from PI unfamiliar surroundings to visual route following in familiar terrain.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the model from prior work.

claim: Ring attractor (RA) circuits in the FB provide an ideal substrate for optimally integrating cues that exist within a shared context.
source: As a final stage, we revealed how ring attractor (RA) circuits (Touretzky, 2005; Sun et al., 2018; see Figure 1) that we hypothesise exist in the FB provide an ideal substrate for optimally integrating cues that exist within a shared context (e.g. PI and visual homing [VH] in unfamiliar contexts).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations.

claim: The 'copy-and-shift' mechanism 'transfers' orientation outputs into a shared frame of reference.
source: The 'copy-and-shift' mechanism again plays a crucial role in this capacity as it 'transfers' orientation outputs into a shared frame of reference.
evidence: This is stated as a function of the mechanism.

claim: When ascending gradients, temporal changes in visual familiarity are translated into heading commands relative to the head-direction system which then share a frame of reference with the PI system.
source: For example, when ascending gradients, temporal changes in visual familiarity are translated into heading commands relative to the head-direction system which then share a frame of reference with the PI system.
evidence: This is given as an example of the frame-transfer function.

claim: The biologically constrained model of the insect midbrain was shown to be capable of generating realistic visual navigation behaviours of desert ants through the coordinated action of visual route following (RF), VH, and PI modules.
source: This biologically constrained model of the insect midbrain was shown to be capable of generating realistic visual navigation behaviours of desert ants through the coordinated action of visual route following (RF), VH, and PI modules partially addressing two of the requirements listed above (Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work.

claim: Adult and larvae fruit flies readily climb rewarding odour gradients by modulating their heading direction in direct response to the temporal change in odour concentration.
source: Adult and larvae fruit flies readily climb rewarding odour gradients by modulating their heading direction in direct response to the temporal change in odour concentration (Gomez-Marin et al., 2010; Nagel and Wilson, 2011; Kim et al., 2011; Schulze et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: The neural pathways of olfactory processing differ from the model only in their sensory origins (antennal lobe [AL] to the lateral horn [LH] and MBs) before connecting to the CX.
source: Moreover, the neural pathways of olfactory processing are well established and only differ from our model in their sensory origins (antennal lobe [AL] to the lateral horn [LH] [Gupta and Stopfer, 2012; Roussel et al., 2014] and MBs [Aso et al., 2014; Hulse et al., 2021]) before connecting to the CX through direct or indirect (hypothetically via superior medial protocerebrum [SMP]; Plath et al., 2017; Hulse et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020) neural pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical work.

claim: By changing the input from optic to ALs and the processing region from the MB to the LH and MB, the model is able to adapt its heading to align with the positive odour gradient over successive steps.
source: Thus by simply changing the input from optic to ALs and the processing region from the MB to the LH and MB (see Figure 2A, left panel) our model is able to adapt its heading to align with the positive odour gradient over successive steps (see Figure 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the model with reference to figures.

claim: The model generates realistic chemotaxis behaviour in a classic 'volcano' environment.
source: Figure 2C (left panel) demonstrates the realistic chemotaxis behaviour generated by the model in a classic 'volcano' environment (Jung et al., 2015; Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with reference to a figure and citations to prior work.

claim: There are neural pathways not included in the model that directly link odour input to motor outputs that may play a role in chemotactic guidance.
source: It should be noted that there are neural pathways not included in the model that directly link odour input to motor outputs that may play a role in chemotactic guidance (Green et al., 2019; Rayshubskiy, 2020; Scaplen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation with citations.

claim: Larvae possess MB and LH assemblies but do not have a fully developed CX as modelled.
source: Indeed while larvae possess MB and LH assemblies, they do not have a fully developed CX as modelled here (Gowda et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: In moving airflows, adult fruit flies pinpoint olfactory sources by anemotaxis whereby individuals align with the upwind direction.
source: In moving airflows, adult fruit flies pinpoint olfactory sources by anemotaxis whereby individuals align with the upwind direction, allowing them to approach the hidden odour source (Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; Rutkowski et al., 2009; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Insects sense wind direction through deflections of their antennae.
source: Insects sense wind direction through deflections of their antennae (Yorozu et al., 2009; Patella and Wilson, 2018; Okubo et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The wedge projection neurons (WPNs) convert antennal inputs into a direction relative to the animal's current heading.
source: with the wedge projection neurons (WPNs) converting their inputs (via antennal mechanosensory and motor centre [AMMC] pathway in Figure 2B, right panel) into a direction relative to the animal's current heading (Suver et al., 2019; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to figures.

claim: The WPN output is transmitted to the FB of the CX via the lateral accessory lobe (LAL) -> noduli (NO) pathway.
source: The WPN output is then transmitted to the FB of the CX via the lateral accessory lobe (LAL) -> noduli (NO) pathway (Hulse et al., 2021; Matheson et al., 2021; Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to figure.

claim: By driving the direction and magnitude of the 'shift' by the WPN response when a rewarding odour is detected, the model turns the agent upwind.
source: By simply driving the direction and magnitude of the 'shift' by the WPN response when a rewarding odour is detected (Figure 2A, right panel), the model turns the agent upwind (see Figure 2B, right panel).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the model with reference to figures.

claim: The model demonstrates realistic odour-driven anemotaxis behaviour in a classic laboratory environment with an odour plume.
source: Figure 2C (right panel) shows an example path of a simulated fly navigating a classic laboratory environment with an odour plume into which rewarding odour is toggled ON and OFF (for a simulation of a group agents, see Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which demonstrates realistic odour-driven anemotaxis behaviour.
evidence: This is stated with reference to figures.

claim: The model generalizes from visual to olfactory navigation without significant alteration.
source: Taken together the above data demonstrate the capacity of the model to generalise from visual to olfactory navigation without significant alteration.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the chemotaxis and anemotaxis results.

claim: Across species and environments, a distinct behavioural trigger is reported at the onset (ON response) or loss (OFF response) of sensory valence.
source: Across species and environments (laminar odour gradient or turbulent odour plume), a distinct behavioural trigger is reported at the onset (ON response) or loss (OFF response) of sensory valence (moths [Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; Rutkowski et al., 2009], flying fruit flies [van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014], walking flies [Steck et al., 2012; Bell and Wilson, 2016; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies across species.

claim: In the presence of attractive odour, animals apply anemotaxis and surge upwind.
source: Specifically, in the presence of the attractive odour animals apply anemotaxis and surge upwind, but when the attractive odour is lost they engage in a chemotactic-like search to recover the plume.
evidence: This is stated as a behavioral pattern.

claim: When the attractive odour is lost, animals engage in a chemotactic-like search to recover the plume.
source: Specifically, in the presence of the attractive odour animals apply anemotaxis and surge upwind, but when the attractive odour is lost they engage in a chemotactic-like search to recover the plume.
evidence: This is stated as a behavioral pattern.

claim: The CX switching circuit can be reconfigured to be triggered by the instantaneous change of odour concentration fitting with the reported ON and OFF responses.
source: Figure 3A (left panel) depicts how the CX switching circuit can be easily reconfigured to be triggered by the instantaneous change of odour concentration fitting with the reported ON and OFF responses (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figure and citation.

claim: The ON and OFF responses are driven by the output neurons of the odour processing brain regions (i.e. MBON or LHON) that could compute the temporal changes of odour concentration.
source: Note that we here assume that the ON and OFF responses are driven by the output neurons of the odour processing brain regions (i.e. MBON or LHON) that could compute the temporal changes of odour concentration (Dolan et al., 2018; Hulse et al., 2021; Matheson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption with citations.

claim: The model demonstrates realistic olfactory navigation behaviour similar to the behavioural data in Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018.
source: Figure 3 (left panel) demonstrates realistic olfactory navigation behaviour similar to the behavioural data in Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated with reference to figure and citation.

claim: Homing desert ants follow their path integrator to their nest area before relying on nest odour plumes for their final approach.
source: In barren salt pans, homing desert ants follow their path integrator to their nest area before relying on nest odour plumes for their final approach (Buehlmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior behavioral study.

claim: Ants weigh their PI output relative to the home vector length in a similar fashion to their integration of PI and visual cues.
source: Rather, ants instead appear to weigh their PI output relative to the home vector length in a similar fashion to their integration of PI and visual cues (Wystrach et al., 2015; Legge et al., 2014) as was realised in our previous model using ring attractor networks (Touretzky, 2005; Sun et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral and modeling work.

claim: The model generates homing paths that closely match those of real ants following simulated displacements.
source: Figure 3C shows homing paths generated by the model following simulated displacements left or right of the regular feeder which closely match those of real ants (Buehlmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figure and citation.

claim: The CX possesses the neural mechanisms to flexibly coordinate the various guidance behaviours observed in insects across sensory domains.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that the CX possess the neural mechanisms to flexibly coordinate the various guidance behaviours observed in insects across sensory domains, supporting its role as the navigation centre (Honkanen et al., 2019; Hulse et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citations.

claim: Desert ants travel to and from familiar feeder locations via visually guided routes.
source: Desert ants travel to and from familiar feeder locations via visually guided routes (Kohler and Wehner, 2005; Mangan and Webb, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Wind gusts can blow desert ants off course.
source: Desert ants travel to and from familiar feeder locations via visually guided routes (Kohler and Wehner, 2005; Mangan and Webb, 2012), but wind gusts can blow them off course.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about ant navigation.

claim: In the instant prior to displacement, ants assume a stereotypical 'clutching' pose during which they transfer their egocentric measure of wind direction into a geocentric frame of reference given by their celestial compass.
source: Wystrach and Schwarz, 2013 reported that in the instant prior to displacement ants assume a stereotypical 'clutching' pose during which they transfer their egocentric measure of wind direction (indicating the direction in which they are about to be blown) into a geocentric frame of reference given by their celestial compass.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior behavioral study.

claim: Displaced ants utilize their celestial compass memory to guide their path directly towards their familiar route.
source: Displaced ants then utilise this celestial compass memory to guide their path directly towards their familiar route (Figure 4A, left panel).
evidence: This is stated with reference to figure.

claim: During the clutch pose, the celestial compass heading is copied and shifted by the activation of the WPN encoding the upwind direction relative to the animal's heading to create a desired heading that points back along the direction of travel.
source: That is, during the clutch pose the celestial compass heading is copied and shifted by the activation of the WPN encoding the upwind direction relative to the animal's heading to create a desired heading that points back along the direction of travel.
evidence: This is stated as a model mechanism.

claim: The desired heading is maintained in a working memory during displacement before activation to guide the agent back to the familiar route region.
source: This desired heading is maintained in a working memory during displacement before activation to guide the agent back to the familiar route region (see simulated navigating paths in Figure 4C, left panel).
evidence: This is stated as a model mechanism with reference to figure.

claim: Homing desert ants captured just before entering their nest and released in unfamiliar visual surroundings initially dash back along the celestial compass heading in which they were travelling.
source: Similarly, homing desert ants captured just before entering their nest and released in unfamiliar visual surroundings initially dash back along the celestial compass heading in which they were travelling (Wystrach et al., 2013; Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior behavioral study.

claim: Ants lacking PI cues and displaced from other locations along the route have no preferred direction of travel following displacement.
source: Note that this differs from the behaviour of ants lacking PI cues and displaced from other locations along the route. Those ants have no preferred direction of travel following displacement according to the observation (Wystrach et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior behavioral study.

claim: The sight of the nest surroundings could be considered a 'special circumstance' similar to the 'clutching' pose.
source: This indicates that the sight of the nest surroundings could be considered a 'special circumstance' in a similar way to the 'clutching' pose mentioned above.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from behavioral data.

claim: When there is a significant drop of visual novelty, the compass direction is copied and shifted by 180° to create a new desired heading stored in working memory.
source: Figure 4B (right panel) depicts how this behaviour could also arise from the 'copy-and-shift' mechanism. That is, when there is a significant drop of visual novelty (as might only be experienced after a displacement from the nest), the compass direction is again copied and shifted by a predetermined amount, this case 180°. This creates a new desired heading that can be stored in working memory that will cause the initial search to be focused in the direction from which the animals just travelled (Figure 4C , right panel).
evidence: This is stated as a model mechanism with reference to figures.

claim: The 'copy-and-shift' mechanism can transfer directional cues from an unstable frame of reference such as the wind direction to a stable frame of reference such as the global celestial compass.
source: In summary, the data above demonstrate the flexibility of the 'copy-and-shift' mechanism to transfer directional cues from an unstable frame of reference such as the wind direction to a stable frame of reference such as the global celestial compass which can be used at a later time.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the wind compensation and backtracking results.

claim: The transfer of directional cues is triggered by special sensory experience and motivational state of the animal.
source: We proposed that this transfer is triggered by special sensory experience and motivational state of the animal that could be driven by some of the numerous tangential inputs from multiple upstream brain regions to the FB (Franconville et al., 2018; Hulse et al., 2021) forming a contextually dependent guidance network.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal with citations.

claim: The CX-based steering circuit augmented with a copy-and-shift functionality can generate realistic odour-based chemotaxis and anemotaxis behaviours.
source: To summarise, we have shown how the CX-based steering circuit augmented with a copy-and-shift functionality can generate realistic odour-based chemotaxis and anemotaxis behaviours adding to the PI, VH, visual RF, and long-range migrations explained previously (Stone et al., 2017; Honkanen et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings with citations.

claim: CX-based mechanisms can coordinate guidance cues across sensory domains using biologically realistic context-dependent switches and ring attractor networks.
source: We have also outlined CX-based mechanisms that can coordinate guidance cues across sensory domains using biologically realistic context-dependent switches and ring attractor networks.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings.

claim: The copy-and-shift mechanism can facilitate the transfer of orientation cues between unstable to stable frames of references.
source: Finally, we demonstrated how the copy-and-shift mechanism can facilitate the transfer of orientation cues between unstable to stable frames of references.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings.

claim: By triggering a transfer under specific environmental conditions, insects can increase the robustness of their guidance repertoire.
source: By triggering such a transfer under specific environmental conditions, insects can increase the robustness of their guidance repertoire.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: The model can be considered as a general navigation model extending across multiple behavioural tasks experienced in multiple contexts.
source: The model presented can thus be considered as a general navigation model extending across multiple behavioural tasks (alignment with rotationally varying compass, visual route, or wind cues; and gradient ascent of spatially varying but rotationally invariant cues such as odour and visual memories) experienced in multiple contexts.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the model's generality.

claim: The results add further validation to the claim that the CX acts as the seat of navigation coordination in insects.
source: Taken together the results add further validation to the claim that the CX acts as the seat of navigation coordination in insects.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion.

claim: The CX is as ancient as insects themselves.
source: The CX is as ancient as insects themselves (Homberg, 2008; Strausfeld, 2009) and is highly conserved across different species solving different navigational tasks (Honkanen et al., 2019; Hulse et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The CX is highly conserved across different species solving different navigational tasks.
source: The CX is as ancient as insects themselves (Homberg, 2008; Strausfeld, 2009) and is highly conserved across different species solving different navigational tasks (Honkanen et al., 2019; Hulse et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The fixed circuitry of the CX appears optimised to receive input from a variety of sensory sources and return a similar variety of navigational behaviours applicable across contexts.
source: This fixed circuitry thus appears optimised to receive input from a variety of sensory sources and return a similar variety of navigational behaviours applicable across contexts.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the CX architecture.

claim: 'Bowtie' (or hourglass) architecture is observed in the decision-making circuits of the mammalian brain.
source: Indeed, Doyle and Csete, 2011 posits that such 'bowtie' (or hourglass) architecture is also observed in the decision-making circuits of the mammalian brain (Redgrave et al., 1999; Humphries and Prescott, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bowtie architecture functions by providing 'constraints that deconstrain'.
source: Indeed, Doyle and Csete, 2011 posits that such 'bowtie' (or hourglass) architecture is also observed in the decision-making circuits of the mammalian brain (Redgrave et al., 1999; Humphries and Prescott, 2010) and function by providing 'constraints that deconstrain' (see Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by citation with reference to figure.

claim: The fixed circuitry of the CX constrains the format of the sensory input but deconstrains the application domains of the output behaviours.
source: That is, the fixed circuitry of the CX constrains the format of the sensory input but decontrains the application domains of the output behaviours.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the bowtie architecture.

claim: The model can be considered an example of bowtie structure within the CX.
source: Through interpreting various navigation behaviours through the lens of the 'copy-and-shift' mechanism, our model can be considered an example of such bowtie structure within the CX (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with reference to figure.

claim: Lateralised neural connections and synapse plasticity that shift the head-direction output relative to sensory input have already been mapped.
source: Regarding the copy-and-shift mechanism, lateralised neural connections and synapse plasticity that shift the head-direction output relative to sensory input (i.e. nudge the activation 'bump' within a population of neurons) have already been mapped (Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Green et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2019) and modelled (Cope et al., 2017), demonstrating the feasibility of such computation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Goulard et al., 2021 presented a CX-based navigation model that includes a biologically realistic neural pathway that is functionally similar to the copy-and-shift mechanism proposed here.
source: More recently, Goulard et al., 2021 presented a CX-based navigation model that includes a biologically realistic neural pathway that is functionally similar to the copy-and-shift mechanism proposed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: A short-term memory of a desired heading could be maintained in the FB of the CX via synapse-weight modulation after the original guidance cue is removed.
source: The same study also outlined how a short-term memory of a desired heading could be maintained in the FB of the CX via synapse-weight modulation after the original guidance cue is removed that could support the wind compensation and backtracking behaviours described above.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: A ring attractor network to optimally integrate the desired heading cues could be realised in the complex intra-connections within the FB and the NO.
source: Our model hypothesises the existence of a ring attractor network to optimally integrate the desired heading cues which we suggest could be realised in the complex intra-connections within the FB and the NO (Hulse et al., 2021; Sayre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations.

claim: Different populations of Protocerebral bridge - Fan-shaped body - Nodulus (PFN) neurons in the CX simultaneously store the distinct desired headings computed by the independent navigation systems.
source: We also hypothesise that different populations of Protocerebral bridge - Fan-shaped body - Nodulus (PFN) neurons in the CX simultaneously store the distinct desired headings computed by the independent navigation systems (e.g. PI-based home vector is stored in CPU4 neurons [a subset of PFNs]; Stone et al., 2017; Hulse et al., 2021; Sayre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations.

claim: The hypothetical context switching could be achieved by the recently mapped FB-NOc neurons found in the bees.
source: Further, the hypothetical context switching introduced could be achieved by the recently mapped FB-NOc neurons found in the bees (Sayre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citation.

claim: The simulated odour perception utilised is very simplistic.
source: It is also worth noting that the simulated odour perception utilised here is very simplistic.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: The model assumes that the odour stimulus forms a stable gradient, which reflects laboratory settings but simplifies the spatiotemporally complex plumes in naturalistic settings.
source: For example, we assume that the odour stimulus (with or without a laminar airflow) forms a stable gradient, which while reflecting the laboratory settings in behavioural studies (Gomez-Marin et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018) simplifies the spatiotemporally complex plumes in naturalistic settings where odour encounters are intermittent, occurring randomly as brief bursts (Murlis et al., 2000; Webster and Weissburg, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation with citations.

claim: More stable odour gradients have been mapped to the desert surfaces upon which desert ants forage.
source: We do note, however, that more stable odour gradients have been mapped to the desert surfaces upon which desert ants forage (Buehlmann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Insect olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and projection neurons (PNs) possess adaption and divisive gain control mechanisms that normalise and smooth noisy olfactory inputs.
source: Regardless, insect olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) and projection neurons (PNs) posses adaption (Kaissling et al., 1987; Nagel and Wilson, 2011) and divisive gain control (Luo et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2010; Gorur-Shandilya et al., 2017) mechanisms that normalise and smooth noisy olfactory inputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Visual gradients can often present data in a noisy fashion similar to olfactory inputs.
source: It is interesting to note that the visual gradients can often present data in a similar noisy fashion (personal observation) and thus raises the question as to whether similar processing steps are applied across modalities.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and speculation.

claim: There are shared early sensory processing principles across sensory modalities, especially vision and olfaction in insects.
source: Indeed, this hypothesis is supported by identification of shared early sensory processing principles across sensory modalities (Wilson, 2013), especially the vision and olfactory in insects (Mu et al., 2012) and mammals (Cleland, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both visual and olfactory cues are transferred directly to motor centres providing redundant information streams.
source: Firstly, as well as innervating the CX, both visual and olfactory cues are also transferred directly to motor centres (Rayshubskiy, 2020; Scaplen et al., 2021; Green et al., 2019) providing redundant information streams.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The direct pathways may be used for fast reflex-like movements, whereas the CX pathway is responsible for higher-level guidance that requires learning and integration of multiple elemental guidance systems.
source: One possibility is that the direct pathways are used for fast reflex-like movements, whereas the CX pathway is responsible for higher-level guidance that requires learning and integration of multiple elemental guidance systems (Currier et al., 2020; Matheson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with citations.

claim: The LALs, downstream of the CX, possess neural structures well suited to integrating outputs of the fast and the slow pathways.
source: This view is consistent with Steinbeck et al., 2020, who demonstrate that the LALs, downstream of the CX, possess neural structures well suited to integrating outputs of the fast and the slow pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: For Drosophila larvae, there should be equivalent neural circuitry functioning similarly as the CX involved pathway (probably with the olfactory descending neurons PDM-DN) and direct pathway (probably with odd neurons).
source: For Drosophila larvae, there should be equivalent neural circuitry functioning similarly as the CX involved pathway (probably with the olfactory descending neurons PDM-DN; ; Gowda et al., 2021) and direct pathway (probably with odd neurons; Slater et al., 2015; Gowda et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with citations.

claim: Wind direction sensing from the WPNs is known to feed into the head-direction cells.
source: In this study, we relied solely on the global celestial compass, but wind direction sensing from the WPNs is known to feed into the head-direction cells (Okubo et al., 2020; Hulse et al., 2021), which could facilitate a local compass similar to our previous terrestrial compass.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Le Möel and Wystrach, 2020 and Wystrach et al., 2020 offer the hypothesis that MBs form an opponent memory system that can drive visual RF by balancing the difference in their outputs.
source: Le Möel and Wystrach, 2020 and Wystrach et al., 2020 offer the hypothesis that MBs form an opponent memory system that can drive visual RF by balancing the difference in their outputs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The MBs process rotationally invariant but spatially varying cues (e.g. odour and visual familiarity gradients) and are responsible for generating gradient ascent/descent behaviours such as VH and chemotaxis via operant connections to the CX.
source: Specifically, we propose that the MBs process rotationally invariant but spatially varying cues (e.g. odour and visual familiarity gradients) and are thus responsible for generating gradient ascent/descent behaviours such as VH and chemotaxis via operant connections to the CX.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal about the model's organization.

claim: All rotationally varying cues (e.g. wind direction, visual route memories, and celestial compass) innervate the CX directly via alternate pathways (e.g. LAL).
source: In contrast, all rotationally varying cues (e.g. wind direction, visual route memories, and celestial compass) innervate the CX directly via alternate pathways (e.g. LAL).

claim: The separation of sensory information is fundamental to the flexibility of the model to create the array of behaviours presented.
source: This separation of sensory information is fundamental to the flexibility of the model presented to create the array of behaviours presented and offers a testable hypothesis for future work.
